newsitem.title: THAILAND: Activists campaign to keep Burma out of ASEAN.
newsitem.headline: Activists campaign to keep Burma out of ASEAN.

text.p: Asian human rights activists launched a campaign on Thursday to convince the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to delay accepting Burma into the grouping because of Rangoon's refusal to allow democracy.

The activists ended a two-day "Alternative ASEAN" meeting on Burma with a peaceful demonstration outside the Burmese Embassy in Bangkok to seek the restoration of democracy and human rights in neighbouring Burma.

Carrying pictures of Burmese democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi and placards, the demonstrators pasted the walls of the embassy with political cartoons and slogans against Burma's ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC).

Somchai Homlaor, secretary general of the Asian Forum for Human Rights, told reporters that an Alternative ASEAN Network, supported by over 70 organisations in the region, had been formed to coordinate campaigns against Burma.

ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. The bloc maintains a policy of "constructive engagement" with Burma's military rulers in the hope that such contacts will spark reform within the country.
Burma, which now has observer status in ASEAN, has applied to become a full member at its next formal meeting in July.
Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong, however, said on Thursday that Burma was not yet ready for membership in ASEAN and may be the last of three potential ASEAN members to join.

"I don't think Myanmar (Burma) is quite ready in the near future to adopt all the obligations of being a member of ASEAN," Goh said in an interview for television made available to Reuters by MTV3 Finland.
He said Burma's joining ASEAN depended on its ability to assume certain obligations such as those involving the ASEAN Free Trade Area.
Burma, Laos and Cambodia are the current candidates for membership in ASEAN.

Asked if it was likely Burma would be the last of the three to join ASEAN, Goh said: "I would not know myself at this stage how Myanmar would rank against the Laotions or the Cambodians. But it is possible that Myanmar may be the last member to join ASEAN."
ASEAN's constructive engagement policy came into question earlier this month when Philippine President Fidel Ramos said the group might review that policy.
Thailand's Foreign Minister Amnuay Viravan said on Wednesday that Burma should embrace democracy before becoming a full member of ASEAN.
The activists said they hoped to capitalise on this ASEAN hesitation to thwart Burma's entry into the grouping. ASEAN membership brings some economic privileges.
"ASEAN should delay giving membership status to the SLORC and listen to the voice of the people," Somchai said.

The SLORC in the past has barred access to the home of Nobel Peace laureate Suu Kyi to prevent her from holding meetings of her National League for Democracy (NLD) and has briefly detained hundreds of NLD activists.
The United States and the European Union have imposed travel limitations on senior Burmese leaders, and some Western business interests have launched boycotts of Burmese businesses.
